blocks.html: For any tech, weigh a benefit against a challenge (e.g. telehealth widens rural access but the digital divide excludes some). Privacy answers should name a real safeguard: encryption, documented consent, role-based access, regular audits.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the six roles technology plays in improving health.
revisionQuestions.a: Measure (wearables like Fitbits tracking heart rate and steps), Communicate (telehealth consultations), Monitor (smart inhalers, continuous glucose monitors), Early diagnosis (AI reading medical imaging), Precision (robotic-assisted surgery), and Assist (3D-printed implants and prosthetics).

revisionQuestions.q: Discuss AI's role in healthcare treatment and diagnosis.
revisionQuestions.a: AI reads medical imaging to detect conditions like cancer or heart disease earlier and more accurately than manual review alone, supports drug discovery, and automates administrative tasks — reducing pressure on overworked clinicians while speeding up diagnosis and treatment planning.

revisionQuestions.q: Justify the effectiveness of a new health technology.
revisionQuestions.a: My Health Record is effective because it directly addresses the inefficiency of fragmented, paper-based records — giving GPs, hospitals and pharmacists a shared digital summary of a patient's history, which reduces repeat testing and improves coordination of care.

revisionQuestions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of digital health at connecting health information.
revisionQuestions.a: Tools like My Health Record and ePrescriptions have improved coordination and reduced errors, but effectiveness is limited by inconsistent updating by some professionals and gaps where services aren't fully integrated — so digital health helps significantly but isn't yet a seamless system.

revisionQuestions.q: Discuss a challenge digital health poses for individuals or organisations.
revisionQuestions.a: The digital divide is a key challenge — people without digital literacy, devices or reliable internet access, especially in remote areas, can be excluded from digital health services rather than benefiting from them, widening rather than closing existing health inequities.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how big data is used to reduce health spending.
revisionQuestions.a: Predictive analytics flag at-risk patients for earlier, cheaper intervention instead of late-stage treatment, and reduce unnecessary or duplicate testing — improving the overall efficiency of how health resources are allocated across the system.

revisionQuestions.q: Describe how privacy is protected when big data is used in healthcare.
revisionQuestions.a: Health databases must comply with the Privacy Act 1988 and My Health Records Act 2012, using de-identification of data, encryption, restricted/role-based access controls and regular audits to protect patient information.

  • Assess strategies with health indicators, community feedback & SDG benchmarks

boxes.heading: SDGs in action — the "how" (real-world examples)
boxes.html:
• SDG 3 — remote telehealth programs in outback Australia and rural Africa have widened health access
  • SDG 4 — community education campaigns in sexual health & nutrition across South-East Asia have lowered disease rates
  • SDG 10 — social services in Sweden have narrowed the life-expectancy gap between low- and high-income groups; in Australia, the Closing the Gap campaign targets health, education and economic inequalities between First Nations and non-Indigenous Australians (also a real-world SDG 3 action)
  • SDG 11 — green cities like Copenhagen have reduced pollution and obesity-related illness
  • Local example — Healthy Cities Illawarra: one of the original 1987 Australian pilot sites for the WHO's global Healthy Cities movement; still runs today across Wollongong, Kiama, Shellharbour & the Shoalhaven. Maps directly onto the 4 SDGs — SDG 3: physical activity/nutrition/mental health programs; SDG 4: health literacy workshops in schools; SDG 10: targets low-income families, Aboriginal communities and new migrants; SDG 11: partners with councils on green spaces and walking paths

blocks.html: A top answer names the SDG, states how it's applied with a real example (SDG 3 → remote telehealth in outback Australia; SDG 11 → green cities like Copenhagen), then says how you'd evaluate it — life expectancy, hospitalisation rates, disease prevalence.

revisionQuestions.q: Describe the key features of SDG 3 (Good Health & Wellbeing).
revisionQuestions.a: SDG 3 aims for healthy lives and wellbeing at all ages — its key features include reducing maternal and child mortality, ending epidemics, achieving universal health coverage, reducing non-communicable disease and strengthening mental health services. In Australia this is seen in free vaccination programs and the Closing the Gap campaign.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how SDG 4 relates to SDG 10.
revisionQuestions.a: SDG 4 (Quality Education) raises health literacy, which supports better personal health decisions. SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) partly depends on that education reaching marginalised groups equally, so improving equitable education access is one of the levers that helps narrow health inequality.

revisionQuestions.q: Demonstrate the importance of the SDGs' interrelationship.
revisionQuestions.a: The SDGs are designed to be interconnected — progress on education (SDG 4) supports health outcomes (SDG 3), while sustainable urban planning (SDG 11) supports both by improving access to green space and services. This shows health strategies work best when they address multiple SDGs together rather than in isolation.

revisionQuestions.q: Analyse the effectiveness of Healthy Cities Illawarra as a community health initiative.
revisionQuestions.a: It addresses all four SDGs at once — physical activity and mental health programs (SDG 3), health-literacy workshops in schools (SDG 4), targeted support for low-income, Aboriginal and migrant communities (SDG 10), and council partnerships on green space and walking paths (SDG 11) — showing that multi-sector collaboration is central to its effectiveness.

revisionQuestions.q: Propose a strategy a community could use to advocate for its own health via the SDGs.
revisionQuestions.a: A community could build multi-sector partnerships across health, education, housing and transport, prioritise community leadership (especially Aboriginal co-design), and focus on prevention and early intervention — the same approach Healthy Cities Illawarra uses, adaptable to whatever health issues are most pressing locally.

boxes.heading: Pre-exercise screening
boxes.html:
• Assesses readiness for activity & the need for medical clearance
  • Builds a picture of individual health history
  • Named tools: APEST (Adult Pre-Exercise Screening Tool) and PAR-Q+ — identify existing conditions, injuries & risk factors
  • Lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, stress) let the plan be personalised by age, fitness & limitations
  • Identifies contraindications — reasons to modify or delay an activity — reducing the risk of injury or adverse health events in training

boxes.heading: Building a program
boxes.html:
• Identify baseline fitness, then set SMART goals
  • Match exercise to the client's needs, preferences & limitations
  • Balance intensity, duration & frequency safely
  • Track adaptation and progression over time
  • Common tests — VO₂ max, beep test, 1RM (strength), skinfolds (body composition), Cooper 12-min run
  • Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test — shuttle runs to a beep at rising speed, with a short active-recovery jog between shuttles → measures aerobic fitness and repeated-effort capacity under fatigue (netball, football)
  • Wingate test — a maximal 30-second cycle sprint against fixed resistance → measures anaerobic power and fatigue index (sprint/power sports)

blocks.html: The examiner wants the purpose, not just a list: screening reduces injury risk and personalises the plan. Recreational = motivation & general goals; elite = precise, performance-tracking, injury-prevention. SMART goals make progress measurable.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the importance of pre-exercise health screening.
revisionQuestions.a: Tools like APEST and PAR-Q+ identify existing conditions, past injuries and risk factors before activity begins, reducing the risk of adverse events such as a cardiovascular incident. If a contraindication is found, the activity can be modified or delayed instead of causing harm.

revisionQuestions.q: Analyse how screening supports safe, personalised training.
revisionQuestions.a: By revealing an individual's health history and risk factors, screening lets a program be matched to their age, fitness level and physical limitations, lowering injury risk, while also giving a baseline reading to measure future improvement against.

revisionQuestions.q: Compare fitness testing for recreational versus elite athletes.
revisionQuestions.a: For recreational athletes, testing focuses on health monitoring, motivation and goal setting, and safe program design. For elite athletes, it focuses on performance optimisation, talent identification, and injury prevention and recovery, using more precise sport-specific data like VO₂ max or anaerobic threshold.

revisionQuestions.q: Describe the Yo-Yo test and the Wingate test.
revisionQuestions.a: The Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test uses shuttle runs paced by a beep, with a short active-recovery jog between each, measuring aerobic fitness and repeated-effort capacity under fatigue — useful for team sports. The Wingate test is a maximal 30-second cycle sprint against fixed resistance, measuring anaerobic power and fatigue index.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how exercise assessment assists the development of training programs.
revisionQuestions.a: Baseline testing of cardiovascular endurance, strength, flexibility and body composition establishes a starting point, enables SMART goal setting, and informs which training method suits the athlete (e.g. low anaerobic power might indicate sprint interval training). Regular reassessment then tracks improvement and allows intensity to be adjusted.

revisionQuestions.q: Analyse the importance of identifying contraindications during assessment.
revisionQuestions.a: A contraindication is a health or risk factor meaning an activity should be modified or delayed for safety. Identifying it prevents an unsafe program being built around a risk the athlete or coach wasn't otherwise aware of, which is central to a screening tool's purpose.

boxes.heading: Aerobic (sustained)
boxes.html:
• Improves cardiovascular endurance via the aerobic system
  • Continuous — 30+ min sustained → best for marathon/endurance
  • Fartlek — steady state + sprints → footballers, hockey (variable game demands)
  • Aerobic intervals — moderate intervals → rowers, triathletes
  • Circuit — rotating stations → endurance + strength together

boxes.heading: Anaerobic (high intensity, short)
boxes.html:
• Uses the ATP-PC & lactic acid systems — sprinting, weightlifting, short bursts
  • Anaerobic intervals — repeated hard efforts, short rests → speed & lactate tolerance
  • HIIT (high-intensity interval training) — intense bursts + recovery → anaerobic power & aerobic fitness
  • Plyometrics — jumping/bounding → explosive power (volleyball, netball, AFL)
  • Resistance — strength & power (rugby, rowing, combat)

boxes.heading: The principles of training
boxes.html:
• Progressive overload — gradually ↑ the load to force continued adaptation
  • Specificity — train the energy system & muscles the sport actually uses
  • Reversibility — stop training and adaptations are lost ("use it or lose it")
  • Variety — vary the stimulus to prevent staleness, plateaus & boredom
  • Individuality — tailor the program to the athlete's needs & rate of response
  • Overtraining & recovery — schedule rest so adaptation, not breakdown, occurs

boxes.heading: Thresholds, warm-up & cool-down
boxes.html:
• Aerobic threshold — ~55–85% of max HR: the zone that drives endurance gains
  • Anaerobic threshold — where lactate accumulates faster than it can be cleared
  • Warm-up — raise HR & body temp, dynamic stretch, skill rehearsal → prevents injury
  • Cool-down — light activity returns the body to rest & clears waste (lactic acid)
  • SIT (sprint interval training) vs HIIT — sprint intervals are all-out with long rest; HIIT is 85–95% max heart rate (MHR) bursts

blocks.html: Static = AFTER, dynamic = BEFORE, PNF = greatest ROM. For adaptations, always finish the chain: overload → cardiac hypertrophy → ↓ resting HR → sustain high intensity longer. Naming the adaptation alone won't score the top band. The 12-marker links principle → adaptation → performance. If asked to evaluate a principle across aerobic and strength training, always give one concrete example from each — don't just define the principle once.

revisionQuestions.q: Compare HIIT and SIT.
revisionQuestions.a: HIIT (high-intensity interval training) uses bursts at roughly 85–95% max heart rate with incomplete recovery between efforts. SIT (sprint interval training) uses all-out maximal sprints with longer rest periods — both are anaerobic, but SIT trades volume for near-maximal intensity on each individual effort.

revisionQuestions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of plyometric training for a chosen sport.
revisionQuestions.a: Plyometrics (jumping, bounding) develops explosive power and agility, making it highly effective for sports needing rapid direction change and jump height, such as volleyball or netball. Its high-impact nature means it should be introduced gradually and combined with adequate recovery to manage injury risk.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain progressive overload applied to strength training.
revisionQuestions.a: Gradually increasing resistance, sets or reps forces continued adaptation — for example, an athlete increasing their squat load by 5kg each fortnight so muscles keep being challenged beyond their current capacity rather than plateauing.

revisionQuestions.q: Describe reversibility applied to strength training.
revisionQuestions.a: Strength and muscle size decline once training stops or is significantly reduced, as the body no longer needs to maintain the adaptation. This shows why consistent training matters more than any single high-intensity session.

revisionQuestions.q: Justify the need for variety in aerobic training programs.
revisionQuestions.a: Rotating continuous, fartlek and interval sessions prevents staleness and boredom, and reduces overuse-injury risk from always stressing the same muscles and joints the same way — while still developing the aerobic system overall.

revisionQuestions.q: Analyse the relationship between progressive overload, hypertrophy and performance.
revisionQuestions.a: Progressive overload stresses muscle fibres beyond their current capacity, triggering muscle hypertrophy (fibre growth) as the body adapts. Larger, stronger fibres then improve force production and power output, directly improving performance in strength and power-based sports.

revisionQuestions.q: Discuss how increased stroke volume and oxygen uptake improve performance.
revisionQuestions.a: Aerobic training increases stroke volume (more blood pumped per heartbeat) and VO₂ max (oxygen uptake capacity). Together these improve oxygen delivery to working muscles, allowing an athlete to sustain higher-intensity effort for longer before fatiguing.

boxes.heading: Yearly program phases
boxes.html:
• Pre-season (preparatory, ~6–12 weeks; up to 2–4 months in some sports) — HIGH volume, moderate intensity; a general phase builds the fitness base, then a specific phase adds skills & tactics
  • In-season (competition, ~5–6 months) — ↓ volume, HIGH intensity; strategy & tactics, maintain fitness, peak for games & recover between them
  • Off-season (transition, ~1 month) — ~1 week total rest, then active recovery/cross-training; address weaknesses & rehab injuries
  • Peaking — temporary optimal performance for the key event
  • Tapering — reduce volume/intensity 1–2 wks before → repairs microtears, tops up glycogen, cuts fatigue

• Macrocycle — the full annual plan; mesocycle — a 4–8 week block; microcycle — a 7–10 day block (the most detailed level)
  • Goal setting — personal (individual) vs shared/cohesion (team)
  • Mental imagery, self-talk, relaxation reduce anxiety & sharpen focus
  • Arousal regulation — calm for golf, high energy for sprints; teams use chants or slow breathing

boxes.heading: Why tapering works — metabolic adaptation
boxes.html:
• Aerobic adaptations (mitochondrial & capillary density, haemoglobin) decline slowly once training eases
  • So a large early cut in volume is safe — fitness is retained while accumulated fatigue clears
  • Anaerobic adaptations fade faster → strength athletes use shorter, step tapers
  • Intensity stays high throughout the taper; only volume drops

boxes.heading: Arousal & anxiety
boxes.html:
• Arousal — physiological activation & readiness (not the same as anxiety)
  • Fine motor skills (golf putt, archery) → low arousal is optimal
  • Gross motor skills (weightlifting, tackling) → high arousal is optimal
  • Trait anxiety — a stable personality tendency to feel anxious before every game
  • State anxiety — situation-specific nerves (e.g. only before a grand final)

boxes.heading: Psychological strategies
boxes.html:
• Mental rehearsal / imagery — visualise success at performance speed
  • Relaxation — meditation, progressive muscle relaxation, centred breathing
  • Concentration — focus on the process (the next action), not the outcome
  • Goal setting — SMART goals; personal (individual) vs shared/cohesion (team)

boxes.heading: Warm-up phases (in order)
boxes.html:
• Phase 1 — General — light jog 5–10 min → raise heart rate & body temperature
  • Phase 2 — Stretching — dynamic stretches → increase ROM, reduce injury risk
  • Phase 3 — Callisthenics — sport-specific conditioning exercises
  • Phase 4 — Skill rehearsal — movements & drills specific to the game

boxes.heading: Factors that influence how strategies & tactics are applied
boxes.html:
• Nature of the sport & its rules/structure — set the boundaries for what strategies are even possible
  • Skill level & experience — advanced tactics need players who can execute them under pressure
  • Environmental & game conditions — weather, surface, altitude force in-game adjustments (e.g. shorter passes in wind/rain)
  • Opposition strengths & weaknesses — scouting shapes which tactics a coach chooses
  • Psychological readiness & team cohesion — a strategy only works if the team trusts it and each other
  • Communication & feedback — signals, calls and in-game coaching adjust tactics live
  • Physical conditioning & fatigue — tactics simplify as players tire late in a game

boxes.heading: Role of technology in improving performance
boxes.html:
• Training innovations — resistance bands, reaction lights, altitude chambers, force plates; VR (virtual reality) & AR (augmented reality) simulate game scenarios to sharpen decision-making, reaction time and tactical awareness without physical fatigue; smart resistance machines & VBT (velocity-based training) adjust resistance in real time based on the athlete's force output to target specific muscular adaptations
  • Equipment advances — carbon-fibre running shoes, aerodynamic helmets, smart textiles, anti-gravity treadmills → reduce resistance/injury load or allow earlier-stage training
  • Recording & monitoring — GPS trackers & wearables (load, speed, heart rate), video analysis (technique correction), live data dashboards (real-time coaching decisions)
  • Considerations — cost and access can widen the gap between elite and grassroots athletes; data can be misread without a coach's expertise

blocks.label: the role & impact of technology
blocks.html: Don't just list devices — argue their role: technology enhances skill acquisition (real-time feedback), individualises training (data-informed decisions) and manages load to cut injury risk. Then weigh the impact both ways — faster adaptation and precision vs cost/access inequity between elite and grassroots athletes, and the risk of over-relying on data without a coach's judgement. A strong answer names a specific technology (VR/AR, VBT, GPS) and links it to both a benefit and a limitation.

blocks.label: comparing yearly programs
blocks.html: The classic 12-marker compares a yearly program for an individual vs a group athlete. The single biggest difference is competition frequency: a marathon runner tapers ~2 weeks for one annual race; a soccer team peaks every week and can only use a short mini-taper. For the 5-marker, apply a different psychological strategy to each (individual = imagery + centred breathing; team = shared goals + group relaxation).

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why peaking and tapering timing differs by sport.
revisionQuestions.a: An individual athlete like a marathon runner tapers for around two weeks before a single annual event to peak once. A team-sport athlete competes weekly, so only a short mini-taper is possible between matches — "peaking" is managed match-to-match rather than built toward one key event.

revisionQuestions.q: Compare a yearly training program for an individual versus a group sport.
revisionQuestions.a: Individual pre-season builds aerobic base, general strength and technique; group pre-season builds team fitness, tactical frameworks and trial games. In-season, the individual targets peaking for key events while the team maintains fitness and refines strategy week to week. Both use an off-season for recovery, but the team's is shorter and less individualised.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the Inverted-U Hypothesis.
revisionQuestions.a: Performance improves as arousal rises, up to an optimal point, then declines if arousal goes too high. The optimal level is sport- and skill-specific — high-intensity contact sports need higher arousal than precision sports like archery, and harder skills (e.g. a handstand) need lower arousal than simpler ones.

revisionQuestions.q: Analyse strategies for managing team stress and anxiety.
revisionQuestions.a: Shared goal-setting and group relaxation techniques build collective composure under pressure, while clear communication and trust between teammates reduce the uncertainty that drives state anxiety in high-pressure moments, like a penalty shot or a last-minute play.

revisionQuestions.q: Discuss how opposition strengths and weaknesses shape strategy.
revisionQuestions.a: Scouting an opponent informs tactic selection — in a group sport this might mean man-marking a key attacking player, while in an individual sport it might mean adjusting serve placement or pace based on a known opponent tendency.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how physical conditioning and fatigue affect tactics late in a game.
revisionQuestions.a: As players tire, complex tactics become harder to execute accurately, so coaches often simplify strategy late in a match and use rotations or substitutions to manage workload and maintain tactical discipline.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the role of GPS trackers and video analysis in improving performance.
revisionQuestions.a: GPS trackers record distance, speed and workload to individualise training load and manage injury risk, while video analysis lets coaches break down technique frame-by-frame for correction — turning training decisions from guesswork into data-informed choices.

revisionQuestions.q: Discuss a limitation of using technology to improve performance.
revisionQuestions.a: Cost and access can widen the gap between elite and grassroots athletes who can't afford GPS or VBT systems, and data can be misread or over-relied on without a coach's expertise to interpret it in context.

boxes.heading: Sleep
boxes.html:
• 8–10 hours recommended for adolescents & athletes
  • Plan consistent sleep/wake times; lighter training when sleep-deprived
  • Avoid screens before bed; use a calming nightly routine
  • Mechanism: deep sleep releases growth hormone (muscle repair); poor sleep raises cortisol → inflammation & injury risk (extra sleep improved basketball shooting ~9%)
  • Why: enhances focus, coordination, muscle repair & reaction time → safer movement, fewer injuries

boxes.heading: Nutrition
boxes.html:
• Balanced diet — carbs (energy), protein (repair), fats, micronutrients
  • Fuel before & after training; carb-rich before, protein after
  • Regular eating times; anti-inflammatory foods (berries, leafy greens, omega-3) aid recovery
  • Why: maintains energy, supports muscle growth/repair, lowers injury risk

boxes.heading: Hydration
boxes.html:
• 2–3 L water/day, more in heat or intense sessions; electrolytes for long/high-intensity work
  • Pre: 5–10 mL per kg body weight, 2–4 hrs before. During: 400–800 mL/hour, adjusted for sweat rate & climate. Post: replace 125–150% of fluid lost, since some is lost through sweat/urine even after rehydrating
  • Even 2% fluid loss measurably reduces physical and cognitive performance
  • Monitor — pale-yellow urine = hydrated; watch thirst, dry mouth & fatigue; weigh before/after training to estimate fluid loss
  • Also maintains synovial fluid that lubricates joints for smoother movement
  • Why: maintains blood flow, reduces cramps, prevents overheating, improves concentration

boxes.heading: Nutrient timing & glycemic index (GI)
boxes.html:
• Before (3–4 hr) — low-GI carbs (oats, grainy bread), moderate protein, low fat/fibre → slow, sustained energy
  • During (>60 min) — high-GI carbs, ~30–60 g/hr (gels, banana, sports drink) → fast glucose
  • After — high-GI carbs + protein → refill glycogen & repair muscle

boxes.heading: Carbohydrate loading
boxes.html:
• Who — endurance events lasting >90 minutes only
  • How — raise carbohydrate to ~7–12 g/kg of body weight per day
  • When — across the 36–72 hours before the event
  • Must also taper training, or it won't work — boosts performance ~2–3%

boxes.heading: Key nutrients
boxes.html:
• Electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, Mg) — lost in sweat; depletion causes muscle cramps
  • Iron — makes haemoglobin for O₂ transport; deficiency → early fatigue (esp. female & endurance athletes)
  • Low-GI foods — oats, grainy bread, lentils (slow release)
  • High-GI foods — gels, bananas, white bread (fast release)

boxes.heading: RED-S — Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport
boxes.html:
• Occurs when energy intake is too low for the athlete's training demands
  • Causes hormonal disruption, impaired bone health & poor recovery
  • Affects female athletes most (studies suggest ~25–60% at risk)
  • Managed by matching energy intake to expenditure, with specialist support

boxes.heading: Supplements — protein & creatine
boxes.html:
• Protein powder — convenient extra protein for repair/growth; benefit is real for athletes with high demands, but whole food already meets most needs — no benefit beyond the body's absorption limit
  • How much: ~0.8 g/kg body weight/day maintains most people; resistance-training athletes chasing hypertrophy need ~1.2–1.8 g/kg/day — still achievable through food alone for most
  • Creatine — boosts the ATP-PCR system's phosphate stores → more repeated short, powerful efforts (sprints, lifts); can cause water retention & weight gain, evidence is weaker for endurance events

boxes.heading: Supplements — caffeine & micronutrients
boxes.html:
• Caffeine — a CNS stimulant; ↓ perceived effort, delays fatigue in endurance events; but can raise heart rate, disrupt sleep and cause dependency/anxiety with overuse
  • Micronutrients as supplements — iron and vitamin D correct a diagnosed deficiency effectively; taken without one, they add little benefit and can be harmful in excess
  • Overall: supplements work best alongside a good diet, not instead of one, and should be used under professional/medical guidance

blocks.html: Every answer here should end in a mechanism: sleep → growth hormone → protein synthesis → repair; dehydration → ↓ blood volume → less O₂ to muscles → fatigue. "It's important" scores nothing without the why. For nutrition: low-GI before, high-GI during/after, and carb loading only works with a taper.

revisionQuestions.q: Analyse dietary requirements before, during and after performance.
revisionQuestions.a: Pre-performance favours complex carbohydrates 3–4 hours before, using only familiar foods and tapering food size as the start nears. During performance, sports drinks provide glucose and electrolytes to sustain intensity and replace sweat losses. Post-performance focuses on replacing glycogen and fluid to begin recovery.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain carbohydrate loading and which athletes benefit from it.
revisionQuestions.a: Carbohydrate loading combines a taper in training with a large complex-carbohydrate intake in the week before an event, maximising glycogen stores. It mainly benefits endurance events lasting longer than about 90 minutes, such as marathons, where glycogen depletion would otherwise limit performance late in the event.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how sleep, nutrition and hydration reduce fatigue and prevent injury.
revisionQuestions.a: Sleep supports muscle repair and hormonal balance — poor sleep slows reaction time and raises overuse-injury risk. Adequate protein, iron and calcium prevent deficiency-related fatigue and support bone and muscle recovery. Proper hydration maintains blood volume so oxygen keeps reaching working muscles, since even 2% fluid loss measurably reduces performance.

revisionQuestions.q: Propose a routine to manage sleep, nutrition and hydration around training.
revisionQuestions.a: A pre-sleep routine (stretching, no screens 30–60 minutes before bed) with consistent sleep/wake times; pre-planned meals with protein and carbs timed within 30–60 minutes post-training; and a personalised hydration plan based on sweat rate, monitored via urine colour or pre/post-training weigh-ins.

revisionQuestions.q: Discuss appropriate use of protein supplementation for performance.
revisionQuestions.a: Most people need only about 0.8g/kg/day, achievable through food. Resistance-training athletes chasing hypertrophy need roughly 1.2–1.8g/kg/day, still achievable through diet for most, so supplementation is mainly useful for post-training timing convenience or for vegetarians/vegans who need to combine plant protein sources carefully.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the risks and benefits of caffeine as a performance supplement.
revisionQuestions.a: As a central nervous system stimulant, caffeine lowers perceived effort and delays fatigue in endurance events. Overuse can raise heart rate, disrupt sleep and cause dependency or anxiety — so timing and dosage matter as much as the substance itself.

boxes.heading: Biomechanical principles
boxes.html:
• Motion — linear, angular & general motion: velocity, speed, acceleration, distance, momentum
  • Balance & stability — keeping the line of gravity within the base of support (centre of gravity, base of support)
  • Force — Newton's laws, force application, summation of force, force absorption
  • Fluid mechanics — flotation, buoyancy, drag (fluid resistance), the Magnus effect

boxes.heading: Applying biomechanics
boxes.html:
• Running — relaxed shoulders/hands, upright posture, arms bent ~90°, minimise ground-reaction force → less fatigue
  • Swimming — reduce drag: streamlined body, hips lifted, tight kick, hands "catch" the water
  • Sport-specific — e.g. shifting weight back-to-front in a tennis serve transfers force into racquet speed; reducing rotation load protects a fast bowler's lower back
  • Functional movement — correct lifting technique (bend at hip, wide base, brace core) protects the spine in everyday tasks and gym work (e.g. CrossFit)

boxes.heading: Physiological recovery
boxes.html:
• Cool-down — gradually lowers HR, ventilation & blood distribution back to resting; prevents blood pooling; static stretching realigns muscle fibres
  • Hydrotherapy — CWI (cold water immersion) ↓ inflammation via vasoconstriction, best for DOMS; WWI (warm) ↑ blood flow via vasodilation, relaxes stiff joints; contrast water therapy alternates both to pump blood flow
  • Avoid hydrotherapy on a hot, red, inflamed injury — swelling must be controlled first

boxes.heading: Psychological recovery
boxes.html:
• Reduces cortisol (the stress hormone), improving focus, sleep quality & emotional resilience
  • Meditation/mindfulness — regulates the stress response, builds body awareness
  • Also used: mental rehearsal, yoga, calming music, aromatherapy, journaling, deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation (PMR)
  • Adequate sleep is regarded as the most important recovery strategy overall — but too much can also cause sluggishness

boxes.heading: Training innovations & monitoring
boxes.html:
• Lactate testing — blood-lactate sampling during graded effort sets athlete-specific training zones
  • VR/AR — simulate competition environments & visualise scenarios without physical strain
  • Apps & AI — Strava, TrainingPeaks, Dartfish (video analysis); AI systems like PlayerMaker, Statcast & TacticAI personalise training and flag fatigue
  • Wearables/GPS — heart rate, distance, speed & workload monitoring in real time

boxes.heading: Equipment advances
boxes.html:
• Lighter, more aerodynamic materials (carbon-fibre bikes, foam-cushioned running shoes) improve speed & reduce injury load
  • Smart equipment — sensor-embedded racquets/balls give real-time technique feedback
  • Assistive technology — lightweight wheelchairs & audible balls (sound/vibration cues) widen access for athletes with disability

boxes.heading: Types of injury
boxes.html:
• Direct — from external contact (ball, bat, person); indirect — internal force (sprains, strains)
  • Soft tissue — muscles, ligaments, fascia (tears, sprains, contusions, abrasions)
  • Hard tissue — bones/teeth (fractures, dislocations)
  • Overuse — repetitive stress (tendonitis, bursitis) from poor programming or insufficient rest

boxes.heading: Fracture types
boxes.html:
• Simple (closed) — bone breaks but stays under the skin; compound (open) — bone breaks through the skin
  • Named patterns: greenstick (incomplete, bends), spiral (twisting), comminuted (3+ fragments), transverse (straight across), oblique
  • Dislocation — bone displaced from the joint; ligaments stretch/rupture but the bone itself isn't damaged; never relocate it yourself
  • A subluxation is a bone momentarily "popping out" and returning — still needs rehab even without lasting displacement

boxes.heading: Assessment & soft-tissue management
boxes.html:
• TOTAPS — Talk, Observe, Touch, Active & Passive movement, Skills test
  • Sequence: DRSABCD (Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR, Defibrillation — the crisis check) → STOP (Stop, Talk, Observe, Prevent — on-field) → TOTAPS (complete)
  • RICER for soft tissue — Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Referral — applied in the first 48–72 hours
  • Ice ≈ 20 min every 2 hrs to reduce swelling & pain
  • Avoid HARM in that time — Heat, Alcohol, Running, Massage — each one increases bleeding/swelling and delays healing

boxes.heading: Hard tissue, rehab & return
boxes.html:
• Dislocation — don't relocate; immobilise, ice, seek help
  • Fracture — immobilise (splint/sling), control bleeding, call emergency; RICER only after clearance
  • Rehab — progressive mobilisation → graduated exercise → modified training; cold early, heat later
  • Cold options — ice massage, cold-water immersion, cold sprays/gels (first ~4 days); heat options — moist heat packs, whirlpool/contrast baths, ultrasound, infrared (once bleeding has stopped, ~48 hrs+)
  • Return-to-play — medical clearance, functional testing, monitor re-injury; physically and psychologically ready

boxes.heading: Rehabilitation stages (in order)
boxes.html:
• Progressive mobilisation — gently restore range of movement (active by the athlete, or passive by a practitioner); not during the acute inflammatory phase, and stay pain-free
  • Graduated exercise — static & PNF stretching, then conditioning using overload to rebuild strength and prevent muscle atrophy
  • PNF stretching in rehab — contract the target muscle 3–5s, relax, then stretch further 10–30s (e.g. hamstring, calf) — used within graduated exercise
  • Total body fitness — rebuild all muscle groups & energy systems (pool work, cycling ergometer, light jogging, weights)
  • Training — build sport-specific skills back to pre-injury level; complete once a full session is done pain-free

boxes.heading: Return-to-play & ethics
boxes.html:
• Readiness indicators — elasticity, strength, mobility, pain-free, and balance on the injured limb
  • Named RTP tests — Illinois Agility Test (agility), vertical jump (power), grip strength, circumduction test (shoulder ROM) — chosen to match the injured area & sport
  • Psychological readiness — confidence rebuilt via sport-specific tests (e.g. beep test) & a sports psychologist
  • Ethics — painkillers mask pain (a damage warning) → further injury & prolonged healing; beware pressure to participate

boxes.heading: Performance-enhancing drugs
boxes.html:
• Stimulants — amphetamines, cocaine, ecstasy, ritalin, nicotine, caffeine — ↑ alertness & delay fatigue; risk: ↑ heart rate, anxiety, impaired fine motor skill
  • Anabolic steroids — ↑ muscle size/strength/recovery; risk: liver damage, heart disease, masculinisation in women
  • Human growth hormone (HGH) — ↑ muscle size, mobilises fat for energy; risk: gigantism, diabetes, disfigurement
  • EPO (blood doping) — ↑ red blood cells & oxygen carriage; risk: blood clots, stroke, ↑ blood viscosity
  • Beta blockers — steady the hands in precision sports (archery, shooting, golf); risk: low blood pressure, fatigue
  • Diuretics — used to "make weight"; risk: dehydration, heart & kidney failure; also banned as a masking agent

boxes.heading: Ethical considerations
boxes.html:
• Fairness — PEDs create an uneven playing field for athletes who can't or won't access them
  • Athlete health & safety — pressure from coaches/team doctors to use PEDs or to play through pain
  • Influence on young athletes — elite PED use can normalise drugs over hard work for developing athletes
  • Integrity of sport — undermines competition based on skill, training & effort
  • Age — younger bodies are more vulnerable to PED harm and to pressure from sponsors/peers

boxes.heading: Drug testing
boxes.html:
• WADA sets the banned-substance list (refreshed every 1 January); in Australia, Sport Integrity Australia carries out testing, in- and out-of-competition
  • A Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE) is approved only if: it's medically necessary, doesn't improve performance beyond normal levels, no reasonable alternative treatment exists, and the condition wasn't caused by prior misuse
  • Strict liability — athletes are responsible for anything found in their body, even if it was taken accidentally (e.g. a contaminated supplement)
  • Limitations — testing is expensive (millions of dollars a year), and athletes must track an annually-changing prohibited list

boxes.heading: Painkillers & the doping line
boxes.html:
• Over-the-counter painkillers (e.g. paracetamol) are legal; prescription painkillers by injection are more concerning — they mask the body's damage warning
  • Playing through masked pain risks turning a manageable injury into a worse, prolonged one
  • Anti-inflammatories/painkillers taken for genuine medical treatment can blur into performance enhancement — a real ethical grey area covered by the TUE process

blocks.html: Know the acronyms cold — TOTAPS, DRSABCD, RICER — and the order they're used in. Never relocate a dislocation. Return-to-play answers must include both physical (functional testing) and psychological readiness. For biomechanics questions, name the actual principle (motion / balance & stability / force / fluid mechanics) rather than just saying 'technique'. For drug use, cover all three angles the syllabus wants — health implications, ethics, and drug testing — and use a named example (e.g. steroids, EPO) rather than a vague 'PEDs'.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how biomechanics reduces injury risk in sport.
revisionQuestions.a: Analysing technique — such as landing mechanics in jump sports or bar-path in weightlifting — identifies poor joint alignment or excess load, allowing correction before it causes strain. For example, adjusting a football player's jump-landing technique can reduce ACL injury risk.

revisionQuestions.q: Analyse how biomechanics develops efficient movement.
revisionQuestions.a: Applying physics principles like force, speed and energy conservation to technique — for example correcting overstriding in a running gait, or adjusting shoulder angle in a tennis serve — reduces wasted energy, improving performance and injury prevention together.

revisionQuestions.q: Outline the four biomechanical principles used to analyse sporting movement.
revisionQuestions.a: Motion (linear, angular and general motion — velocity, speed, acceleration, momentum), balance and stability (keeping the line of gravity within the base of support), force (Newton's laws, force application, summation and absorption), and fluid mechanics (flotation, buoyancy, drag and the Magnus effect).

revisionQuestions.q: Describe how reducing drag improves a swimmer's performance.
revisionQuestions.a: Drag is the resisting force opposing forward motion through water. A swimmer reduces it by keeping a streamlined body position with hips lifted, keeping arms and legs close to the body, kicking tightly with pointed toes, and using a 'catch' hand position — all of which lower energy expenditure and sustain movement for longer.

revisionQuestions.q: Justify recovery strategies used for sustained movement and performance.
revisionQuestions.a: Physiological strategies like a cool-down gradually lower heart rate and clear lactic acid, reducing blood pooling and stiffness. Psychological strategies like progressive muscle relaxation lower cortisol and cognitive fatigue. Together they let an athlete recover fully between sessions rather than accumulating fatigue.

revisionQuestions.q: Describe how hydrotherapy aids recovery.
revisionQuestions.a: Cold water immersion causes vasoconstriction, reducing inflammation and soreness — particularly effective for DOMS. Warm water immersion causes vasodilation, increasing blood flow and relaxing stiff joints. Contrast water therapy alternates both to pump blood flow through the tissue. It should not be used on a hot, red, inflamed injury.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why psychological recovery strategies matter as much as physiological ones.
revisionQuestions.a: Hard training raises cortisol and can leave athletes with low concentration, low motivation and higher anxiety. Techniques like meditation, deep breathing and progressive muscle relaxation lower cortisol, improve sleep quality and focus, and help prevent burnout — meaning an athlete who recovers physically but not mentally is still at risk of underperforming or overtraining.

revisionQuestions.q: Discuss how technology can be used to improve training and performance.
revisionQuestions.a: Wearables and GPS track heart rate, distance and workload in real time; apps like Strava and TrainingPeaks let athletes monitor and adjust training; AI systems such as PlayerMaker and TacticAI personalise programs and flag fatigue; and tools like Dartfish support video-based technique correction — together giving coaches and athletes objective data instead of guesswork.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how equipment advances can both improve performance and support inclusion in sport.
revisionQuestions.a: Lighter, more aerodynamic materials (carbon fibre, cushioned foam soles) reduce energy loss and injury load for able-bodied athletes, while assistive technology — lightweight wheelchairs and audible balls with sound or vibration cues — removes physical and sensory barriers so athletes with disability can participate and compete more effectively.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how injuries are classified, with examples.
revisionQuestions.a: Injuries are classified as direct (caused by an external force, e.g. a tackle) or indirect (caused by internal stress, e.g. a hamstring tear from sprinting), and as soft-tissue (RICER-managed, e.g. a sprain) or hard-tissue (e.g. a fracture, requiring immediate medical referral and never relocated on-field). Overuse injuries like tendonitis are a third category, caused by repetitive stress rather than a single incident.

revisionQuestions.q: Distinguish between a simple and a compound fracture, and name two other fracture patterns.
revisionQuestions.a: A simple (closed) fracture breaks the bone but it stays under the skin; a compound (open) fracture breaks through the skin, carrying a higher infection risk. Other named patterns include greenstick (an incomplete break where the bone bends), spiral (from a twisting force), comminuted (three or more fragments), and transverse (a straight break across the bone).

revisionQuestions.q: Describe key rehabilitation stages after an injury.
revisionQuestions.a: Progressive mobilisation restores range of movement pain-free; graduated exercise (including PNF stretching) rebuilds strength using overload while avoiding muscle atrophy; total body fitness rebuilds general conditioning; training returns sport-specific skills, complete once a full pain-free session is achieved.

revisionQuestions.q: Justify the need for both RICER and HARM guidance in the first 48–72 hours.
revisionQuestions.a: RICER (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Referral) actively limits swelling and bleeding, while HARM (avoid Heat, Alcohol, Running, Massage) prevents actions that would worsen bleeding and swelling during the same window — together they cover both what to do and what to avoid.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how physical tests are used to determine an athlete's readiness to return to play.
revisionQuestions.a: Tests are chosen to match the injured area and sport — for example the Illinois Agility Test for a knee-ligament injury, a vertical jump for muscular power, grip strength for an upper-limb injury, or a circumduction test for a shoulder. Results are compared against a pre-injury baseline or the uninjured limb, and the athlete must be pain-free and demonstrate near-full strength and range of motion before being cleared.

revisionQuestions.q: Discuss the ethical considerations of performance-enhancing drug use.
revisionQuestions.a: PED use undermines fair competition, since not all athletes can or will access them, and pressures other athletes to use them just to stay competitive. It also raises athlete health and safety concerns, particularly where coaches or team doctors apply pressure, and sends a harmful message to young, impressionable athletes that success requires artificial enhancement rather than legitimate training.

revisionQuestions.q: Outline the health risks associated with three different categories of performance-enhancing drugs.
revisionQuestions.a: Anabolic steroids can cause liver damage, heart disease and masculinisation in female athletes. EPO (blood doping) increases blood viscosity, raising the risk of blood clots and stroke. Diuretics cause dehydration and can lead to heart and kidney failure, despite being used to make weight in weight-category sports.

revisionQuestions.q: Describe WADA's role in drug testing.
revisionQuestions.a: The World Anti-Doping Agency sets the list of prohibited substances and methods internationally, refreshed every 1 January. In Australia, Sport Integrity Australia carries out the actual testing — in- and out-of-competition, random and targeted, including biological passports that track markers over time.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the concept of strict liability in drug testing.
revisionQuestions.a: Athletes are held responsible for any banned substance found in their body, even if it was taken accidentally — such as through a contaminated supplement — meaning there's no automatic excuse for a positive test. This is why a food-first, batch-tested approach to supplements matters.

revisionQuestions.q: Outline the criteria used to approve a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE).
revisionQuestions.a: A TUE is only approved if the medication is medically necessary, does not improve the athlete's performance beyond normal levels, no other reasonable treatment exists, and the medical issue was not caused by the athlete's own prior misuse of the medication.

revisionQuestions.q: Discuss why using painkillers to manage an injury raises both a health and an ethical concern.
revisionQuestions.a: Health: painkillers mask pain that signals tissue or organ damage, so an athlete can worsen an injury without realising it, extending recovery time or causing permanent damage. Ethics: the pressure to use painkillers to keep playing important matches usually comes from coaches, teammates or the athlete's own career pressure, raising questions about whether the choice is genuinely free or coerced.

writingScaffolds.label: Short Answer — 2–4 marks (Section II)
writingScaffolds.introNote: These are single-part questions. The command verb and the mark value tell you exactly how much to write. Match the depth to the marks — one clear point per mark.

steps.heading: Read the verb first
steps.html:
Outline = state the main features briefly. Describe = state + add characteristics/detail. Explain = state + say how/why (the mechanism). The verb sets the ceiling on your marks.

📝 Verb → depth Outline (2 marks) = 1–2 precise sentences · Describe (3 marks) = the feature + its detail/example · Explain (4 marks) = the point + mechanism + a consequence.

steps.heading: One idea per mark
steps.html: A 3-mark question needs three distinct, credit-worthy points. Don't repeat the same idea in different words — markers award separate points.

steps.heading: Always finish the chain
steps.html: For Explain, never stop at naming a fact — link it to a mechanism and then a result. "Fact → because → therefore" scores the top mark.

writingScaffolds.modelAnswer:
Question (4 marks): Explain how one anaerobic training method could improve a 100-metre sprinter's performance.

Plyometric training — repeated maximal jumps and bounds such as depth jumps and hurdle hops — overloads the fast-twitch muscle fibres and the stretch-shortening cycle (POINT + METHOD). Because sprinting relies almost entirely on the ATP-PC energy system for short, explosive efforts, this training is specific to the event's demands (MECHANISM). Over time it increases the sprinter's rate of force development and stride power (ADAPTATION), so they accelerate faster out of the blocks and reach a higher top speed (PERFORMANCE RESULT).

writingScaffolds.label: Extended Answer — 6–10 marks (Section II, usually parts a & b)
writingScaffolds.introNote: These questions almost always split into (a) and (b). Treat each part as its own question — the marks are awarded separately, so answer part (a) fully before starting (b).

steps.heading: Split by the marks
steps.html:
A "(a) 4 · (b) 6" question is really two answers. Give part (a) about a paragraph, and spend the most time on the higher-mark part (b).

📝 Rule of thumb 2 marks ≈ 1–2 sentences · 4 marks ≈ a full paragraph with an example · 6 marks ≈ two developed points, each with an example.

steps.heading: Use a named example in every part
steps.html: HMS rewards applied knowledge. Name a real sport, athlete type, scheme or technology in each part — a generic answer caps in the middle band.

steps.heading: Discuss / Analyse need a judgement
steps.html:
If the verb is Discuss or Analyse, description alone won't reach the top band. Weigh strengths against limitations and end with a judgement sentence.

📝 Judgement sentence "Overall, [strategy] is most effective when… but is limited by…, so it works best alongside…"

writingScaffolds.modelAnswer:
Question: (a) Outline the roles of the three levels of government in Australia's healthcare system. (3 marks) (b) Explain how Medicare supports both access and equity. (4 marks)

(a) The federal government funds and regulates the system nationally, running Medicare and the PBS and setting health policy. State and territory governments deliver frontline services — they run public hospitals and emergency care. Local governments handle community-level health, such as immunisation programs, health promotion, and environmental health like clean water and waste. (Three distinct roles = 3 marks.)

(b) Medicare supports ACCESS by providing universal care: any citizen or resident can see a bulk-billing GP or be treated in a public hospital regardless of their ability to pay, removing cost as a barrier to essential treatment. It supports EQUITY through the Medicare Safety Net, which gives extra financial help to people who need frequent care — often the chronically ill or low-income earners — so those with the greatest need receive the most support. By funding care through the income-based Medicare levy, the system spreads cost according to capacity to pay, further improving fairness. (Access + equity each explained with a specific mechanism = 4 marks.)

writingScaffolds.label: Extended Response — 12 marks (Section III, stimulus-based)
writingScaffolds.introNote: Section III has two 12-mark questions — one from Focus Area 1, one from Focus Area 2 — each with a stimulus (an infographic, data table or scenario). The single biggest marks-winner is referring explicitly to the stimulus throughout your answer.

steps.heading: Read the stimulus first — and use it
steps.html:
Underline 2–3 concrete details in the stimulus (a statistic, a scenario detail) and build your answer around them. The rubric explicitly rewards using the stimulus and relevant examples.

📝 Rubric wants Apply knowledge & understanding · apply critical thinking · use relevant examples/concepts/terms · present a logical, cohesive response.

steps.heading: INTRO — define + address the framing
steps.html: Define the key terms and directly name the question's framing — "to what extent" or "evaluate" — so the marker sees you're answering the actual question.

steps.heading: BODY — 2–3 points, each tied back to the stimulus
steps.html: Each paragraph = one point, developed with a mechanism and an example, then explicitly linked to a detail in the stimulus.

steps.heading: JUDGEMENT — answer "to what extent" / "evaluate"
steps.html: Don't sit on the fence. State how far the strategy/advice helps, and name what limits it.

steps.heading: CONCLUSION — 2 sentences that resolve the framing

writingScaffolds.modelAnswer:
Stimulus: The town of "Riverton" — 31% of youth overweight (state avg 24%), 1 in 4 in high psychological distress, 38% of households in the lowest income bracket, only 29% play weekly sport, and just 0.6 GPs per 1,000 people. Question: To what extent could SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) assist in improving the health status of young people in Riverton?

INTRODUCTION The Sustainable Development Goals are global targets that guide health and equity. Riverton's data shows clear disadvantage — high obesity, psychological distress, low income and poor healthcare access. SDG 3 and SDG 10 could substantially improve young people's health, but only to the extent that local barriers of income and service access are also addressed.

SDG 3 — GOOD HEALTH AND WELLBEING SDG 3 targets universal health coverage and the reduction of non-communicable disease and poor mental health. Applied to Riverton, it justifies investment in the GP shortage (0.6 vs 1.2 per 1,000) and youth mental-health services, directly targeting the "1 in 4 in high distress" figure. Programs promoting physical activity would address the low 29% sport-participation rate, reducing the 31% overweight figure over time. To this extent SDG 3 is highly relevant, because it maps onto Riverton's specific health deficits.

SDG 10 — REDUCED INEQUALITIES However, Riverton's problems are rooted in disadvantage: 38% of households are in the lowest income bracket, a socio-economic determinant that drives poor diet, inactivity and distress. SDG 10 addresses this by reducing income and social inequality — for example, subsidised sport, free school-based health programs, and better-funded local services. Without tackling this underlying inequality, SDG 3 health services alone would be underused, so the two goals are most powerful applied together.

JUDGEMENT The goals could improve Riverton's youth health to a significant extent, but not fully on their own. SDG 3 treats the visible health outcomes while SDG 10 addresses the socio-economic cause; the improvement depends on implementing both, and on sustained local funding and community engagement.

CONCLUSION SDG 3 and SDG 10 are highly applicable to Riverton because its poor health outcomes are tied to measurable inequality. Used together — services plus equity — they offer a realistic path to improving young people's health, provided the strategies are properly resourced and community-led.
